Description: explicit — GeoJSON vs tiles decision for a real scenario
prompt: I have about 8,000 hiking trail segments stored as GeoJSON, and users need to click a trail to see its name and distance. I also need a basemap showing terrain and roads. How should I set up the data sources in MapLibre — do I need vector tiles, or can I use GeoJSON?

Description: implicit — dataset outgrew GeoJSON without the user naming tiles
prompt: My parcel layer is a 180 MB GeoJSON file with around 400,000 polygons. The browser hangs for ages on load and sometimes the tab just dies. I've already tried minifying the JSON. What now?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
### TL;DR Your 180 MB / ≈ 400 k-polygon GeoJSON is well beyond the practical limits of a **`geojson` source** (the “crash zone”). The only reliable way to get a smooth, responsive MapLibre map is to **serve the data as tiles** – most commonly **vector tiles (MVT/MLT)** – and keep the GeoJSON only for very small, interactive subsets. Below is a step-by-step plan, plus the “why” and a few quick-win tricks you can try before you go full-tiling. --- ## 1. Why GeoJSON Won’t Work Here | Size / Feature count | Typical browser behaviour | |----------------------|---------------------------| | **< 2 MB / < 5 k features** | Instant load, smooth interaction | | **5 – 20 MB / ≤ 50 k features** | 1–3 s parse delay, mobile may stutter | | **> 50 MB / > 100 k features** | **High risk of freeze or crash** – exactly where you are | *MapLibre must download **the whole file**, parse the entire JSON, build a huge in-memory feature collection, and then render it. Even with minification you still have to transfer 180 MB and allocate a massive JavaScript object. The browser’s garbage collector will thrash, and the UI thread will be blocked for seconds (or minutes) while the parser runs.* --- ## 2. The Correct Solution: Tile the Data ### 2.1. Vector tiles (the default choice) *Pros* * Only the geometry that falls inside the current viewport and zoom level is fetched. * Tiles are tiny (often < 10 KB each) – a 180 MB dataset can shrink to a few hundred MB of tiles, or less with proper simplification. * Styles are client-side, so you keep full interactivity (click, hover, feature-state). * Features remain queryable (`queryRenderedFeatures`, `querySourceFeatures`). *Cons* * You need a tile-generation step and a place to host the tiles (static file server, CDN, PMTiles, etc.). * You must add a `vector` source to your style and reference the appropriate `source-layer`. ### 2.2. Raster tiles (only if you **don’t need** interactivity) If you only need a visual overlay (e.g., a static “heat-map” of the polygons) you could pre-render the polygons to raster tiles (PNG/WebP) and serve them as a `raster` source. You lose click/hover and attribute access, but the browser treats them like any other image layer. > **Bottom line:** For any map where you want to click a polygon, show a popup, or filter by attribute, **vector tiles are the way to go**. --- ## 3. Quick-Start Vector-Tile Workflow | Step | What to do | Tools / Docs | |------|------------|--------------| | **3.1. Simplify & Reduce Precision** | Reduce coordinate precision (e.g., 6-decimal places ≈ 0.1 m) and optionally simplify geometry (e.g., Douglas-Peucker). | `mapshaper` (`-simplify 0.5 -precision 6`), `ogr2ogr -simplify`, or `tippecanoe --simplify` | | **3.2. Split into Logical Layers (optional)** | If you have multiple attribute groups, split into separate GeoJSON files – each becomes its own `source-layer`. | `ogr2ogr`, `mapshaper` | | **3.3. Generate Vector Tiles** | Convert the (now smaller) GeoJSON into an MBTiles/PMTiles archive or a directory of `{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf` files. | **Tippecanoe** (fast, works on any OS)
`tippecanoe -o mydata.mbtiles --drop-densest-as-needed --maximum-zoom=14 --minimum-zoom=5 mydata.geojson`
**Planetiler** (Java, good for OSM-style pipelines) | | **3.4. Host the Tiles** | • **Static file server / CDN** (e.g., Netlify, Vercel, Cloudflare Workers)
• **PMTiles** – a single file you can serve via HTTP range requests (no server needed)
• **Tile server** (tileserver-gl, TileServer-PHP, TileServer-GL-Lite) if you need TileJSON metadata | See the **maplibre-pmtiles-patterns** skill for a zero-ops serverless setup | | **3.5. Wire the Source in MapLibre** | Add a `vector` source that points at the tile URL (or `pmtiles://…`). Then add layers that reference the `source-layer` name you gave in tippecanoe (`--layer=name`). | Use the **maplibre-source-wiring** skill for the exact JSON syntax | | **3.6. Style & Interact** | Write style rules (fill, line, etc.) and enable `click` handlers (`map.on('click', …)`). | MapLibre Style Spec → `paint`/`layout` properties | #### Example: Minimal tippecanoe command ```bash # 1️⃣ Simplify & round coordinates (optional but recommended) mapshaper mydata.geojson -simplify 0.5 -precision 6 -o simplified.geojson # 2️⃣ Build an MBTiles archive (zoom 5-14, 256 px tiles) tippecanoe \ --output=mydata.mbtiles \ --layer=polygons \ --minimum-zoom=5 \ --maximum-zoom=14 \ --drop-densest-as-needed \ --simplify-only-low-zoom \ simplified.geojson ``` *`--drop-densest-as-needed`* tells tippecanoe to automatically prune the most detailed features when a tile would exceed the size limit (default 500 KB). This keeps tile sizes sane even for very dense datasets. #### Example: Adding the source in MapLibre ```javascript map.addSource('my-polygons', { type: 'vector', url: 'https://my.cdn.com/tiles/{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf' // or 'pmtiles://mydata.pmtiles' }); map.addLayer({ id: 'polygons-fill', type: 'fill', source: 'my-polygons', 'source-layer': 'polygons', // name you gave tippecanoe with --layer paint: { 'fill-color': '#ff6600', 'fill-opacity': 0.4 } }); ``` --- ## 4. If You Must Stay in the Browser (No Server) For quick prototyping you can **tile on the client** with `geojson-vt` (or the MapLibre-built-in `GeoJSONSource` with `cluster: true` for points). This splits the GeoJSON into vector-tile-like chunks **in memory**, but it still has to load the whole 180 MB file first – so you’ll still hit the same download-time problem. It’s only useful when the source file is already small enough to download quickly. > **Bottom line:** client-side tiling does **not** solve the “large file download” problem. You still need a smaller payload, i.e., server-side tiles. --- ## 5. Alternative “quick-win” tricks (only if you can’t tile right now) | Trick | What it does | When it helps | |-------|--------------|---------------| | **Chunked loading** | Split the GeoJSON into several smaller files (e.g., by region or zoom level) and load only the needed chunk(s) via `map.addSource` when the user pans/zooms. | Very limited – you still need logic to decide which chunk to load, and you lose seamless interaction. | | **Web Workers for parsing** | Offload the JSON parsing to a worker (`new Worker('parse.js')`). | Reduces UI-thread blocking, but memory usage stays huge; the browser may still OOM. | | **Feature-property reduction** | Drop any properties you never use (e.g., keep only `id` and a few attributes). | Can shave a few MB, but not enough for 180 MB. | | **Use `simplify` on the fly** | Libraries like `simplify-geojson` can thin out geometry after download. | Still requires the full download first; not a real fix. | These are **band-aid** at best. The robust, production-grade solution is tiling. --- ## 6. Hosting Options (so you don’t have to run a full tile server) | Option | How it works | Cost / Complexity | |--------|--------------|-------------------| | **Static CDN (directory of `{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf`)** | Upload the tile folder to any static-file host (Netlify, Vercel, Cloudflare Pages). MapLibre fetches tiles via HTTP. | Free tier usually enough; just need to generate the folder once. | | **PMTiles + Cloudflare Workers / S3** | A single `.pmtiles` file is stored; a small edge worker serves range requests. | Very low overhead; see the **maplibre-pmtiles-patterns** skill for a ready-made worker. | | **TileServer-GL / TileServer-GL-Lite** | Small Node/Go server that reads MBTiles and serves TileJSON + tiles. | Good for local dev or self-hosted infra; a bit more ops. | | **MapTiler Cloud / OpenFreeMap** | Hosted vector-tile services (pay-as-you-go). You upload your MBTiles and they serve them globally. | No ops, but costs scale with traffic. | | **Planetiler (Java) + Cloud storage** | If you need a repeatable pipeline (daily updates), Planetiler can generate tiles directly into an S3 bucket. | Higher engineering effort, but fully automated. | Pick the simplest that fits your deployment timeline. For a one-off demo, **upload the MBTiles to a public S3 bucket and enable static website hosting** – MapLibre can read it via `url: 'https://s3.amazonaws.com/bucket/mydata/{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf'`. --- ## 7. Recap – What to Do Next 1. **Simplify & round** the original GeoJSON (use `mapshaper` or `ogr2ogr`). 2. **Generate vector tiles** with **Tippecanoe** (or Planetiler if you prefer Java). 3. **Host the tiles** – easiest is a static CDN or a PMTiles file served via a Cloudflare Worker. 4. **Add a `vector` source** to your MapLibre style and style the polygons as you like. 5. (Optional) If you need **terrain** or **satellite imagery**, add a `raster` or `raster-dem` source alongside the vector source – they can coexist without any extra work. Once you have the tiles in place, the browser will only ever download a few kilobytes per tile, the UI stays responsive, and you retain full interactivity (click, hover, filter, etc.). --- ### Further Reading / Tools | Category | Resource | |----------|----------| | **GeoJSON simplification** | | | **Vector-tile generation** | Tippecanoe:
Planetiler: | | **PMTiles** | (includes a Cloudflare Worker example) | | **MapLibre source wiring** | `maplibre-source-wiring` skill (layer order, `source-layer`, CORS) | | **Style spec** | | | **Offline single-file demo** | Use a PMTiles archive + `pmtiles://` URL – works even without network after the file is cached. | If you run into any specific hiccup while generating the tiles (e.g., “tile size exceeds limit”, “source-layer not found”), let me know the exact error and I can walk you through the fix. Happy tiling!

Description: anti-pattern — merging basemap and application data into one tileset
prompt: I want my roads, water, labels, and my own delivery-zone polygons all in a single vector tileset so the map only hits one source. What's the best pipeline to merge OpenStreetMap data with my polygons and build that combined tileset?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
**Short answer** > You don’t need a “single-source” tileset to get good performance. > The usual, recommended pattern is **one vector-tile source for the basemap (roads, water, labels, etc.)** + **a second source for your delivery-zone polygons** (either a small GeoJSON that MapLibre reads directly, or your own vector-tile source if the polygons are large). MapLibre will request both sources in parallel, and there is no rendering penalty for having two sources. In fact, keeping the basemap separate avoids a lot of hidden costs (re-building the whole world every time you add a few polygons, licensing headaches, loss of style flexibility, etc.). Below is a concise guide that covers: 1. **Why the two-source pattern is usually the right choice** 2. **When a single combined tileset *is* justified** (offline/kiosk use-cases) 3. **The high-level pipeline you could use if you really want to merge OSM data with your polygons** – just the tools and references, not a step-by-step script (the skill “maplibre-source-wiring” will show you how to wire the sources into a style). --- ## 1️⃣ Why you normally keep the basemap separate | Reason | What happens if you merge everything | What happens with two sources | |--------|--------------------------------------|------------------------------| | **Update frequency** | Any change to your polygons forces a full rebuild of the whole OSM tileset (planet-scale or at least a regional extract). | You rebuild *only* the delivery-zone tiles (or just keep them as GeoJSON). | | **Attribution & licensing** | You become a redistributor of OSM data; you must carry OSM’s attribution on every tile and respect any downstream license constraints. | You consume the basemap from a provider that already handles attribution (e.g., OpenFreeMap, MapTiler, or a public OSM vector tile service). | | **Style flexibility** | The style is baked into the tiles; you cannot change road colours, label fonts, or turn layers on/off without re-generating tiles. | The basemap stays a vector source, so you can re-style it on the client at will, while your own polygons stay independent. | | **Build & storage cost** | A combined tileset is larger (you’re storing OSM geometry *plus* your polygons in the same MVT files). | You only store the extra polygons once, and you can use a hosted basemap that already has compression optimised. | | **Network efficiency** | The client still has to download the same amount of data (OSM tiles + your polygons) – you just lose the ability to cache the basemap separately. | Browsers cache the basemap tiles independently; your small overlay may be cached for a much longer time or even stay in-memory as GeoJSON. | Because MapLibre requests all sources concurrently, there is **no per-source rendering penalty**. A style can list dozens of sources without any slowdown beyond the network cost of the tiles themselves. --- ## 2️⃣ When a single combined tileset *does* make sense | Situation | Why a single tileset is acceptable | Recommended approach | |-----------|-----------------------------------|----------------------| | **Offline / air-gapped kiosk** | No network at all; you need one file (or one archive) that contains everything the map will ever show. | Build a *self-contained* PMTiles (or MBTiles) archive that includes both the basemap and your polygons. | | **Demo / proof-of-concept** where you want to ship a single file to a colleague. | Simplicity of distribution outweighs the rebuild cost. | Same as above – a single PMTiles/MBTiles file. | | **Very small region** (e.g., a single city) where the basemap extract is only a few hundred MB and you already have a pipeline for generating it. | The extra storage and rebuild effort is negligible. | Merge OSM extract + your polygons into one vector-tile set. | Even in those cases you still **keep the two logical sources inside the same tileset** (i.e., separate source-layers for “osm-roads”, “osm-water”, “osm-labels”, “delivery-zones”). That way you can style them independently in the MapLibre style. --- ## 3️⃣ High-level pipeline to *merge* OSM data with your polygons (if you decide you really need a single tileset) > **Do not write a full script here** – the skill is only about *choosing* the source type. Below are the *tools* you would use, plus the key steps you’d follow. For the exact command-line flags, see each tool’s documentation (linked). | Step | What you need to do | Typical tool(s) | |------|---------------------|-----------------| | **a. Get an OSM extract** | Download the region you care about (planet, continent, country, or custom polygon). | `osmconvert`, `osmfilter`, or directly from providers like Geofabrik, BBBike, or the OSM “planet” dump. | | **b. Prepare your delivery-zone polygons** | Convert your polygons to a format that the tiling tool can read (GeoJSON, Shapefile, or FlatGeobuf). Simplify if they are very detailed. | `ogr2ogr` (GDAL) → GeoJSON, optionally run `mapshaper` for simplification. | | **c. Merge the two datasets** | Combine the OSM data and your polygons into a single vector data source. | `ogr2ogr` (append), `osm2pgsql` (load OSM into PostGIS then `INSERT` your polygons), or simply concatenate GeoJSON files if you’re using tippecanoe. | | **d. Choose a tiler** | Generate MVT (Mapbox Vector Tile) or MLT (MapLibre Tile) files from the merged data. | • **tippecanoe** – fast, works directly on GeoJSON/TopoJSON.
• **Planetiler** – Java-based, good for large OSM extracts and custom layers.
• **tilemaker** – C++ tool that can read OSM PBF and output MVT. | | **e. Define layer names (source-layers)** | In the tiler config, give each logical group a distinct `source-layer` name (e.g., `osm_roads`, `osm_water`, `osm_labels`, `delivery_zones`). | tippecanoe `--layer` flag, Planetiler `Layer` definitions, tilemaker `layer` config. | | **f. (Optional) Package as PMTiles/MBTiles** | Bundle the generated tiles into a single archive that MapLibre can read via the `pmtiles:` or `mbtiles:` protocol. | **pmtiles** CLI (`pmtiles create …`), **mbutil**, or **tile-join** from tippecanoe (`--output=tiles.pmtiles`). | | **g. Host the tiles** | Serve the archive (or the tile directory) via a static HTTP server, a CDN, or a serverless function that implements the PMTiles protocol. | `pmtiles` server (Node/Go), `tileserver-gl`, `tileserver-php`, Cloudflare Workers, AWS Lambda, etc. | | **h. Wire the source into a style** | Add a `vector` source that points at the tile URL (or `pmtiles://…`). Reference the appropriate `source-layer`s in your layers. | See the **maplibre-source-wiring** skill for the exact JSON shape. | | **i. Add attribution** | If you redistributed OSM data, you must display OSM attribution (and any other data source attribution). | Add an `attribution` field to the source or a separate UI element. | ### Quick “cheat-sheet” command examples (for reference only) ```bash # 1️⃣ Download OSM extract (e.g., a .pbf for a country) wget https://download.geofabrik.de/europe/germany-latest.osm.pbf -O germany.osm.pbf # 2️⃣ Convert your delivery zones to GeoJSON (if they are in Shapefile) ogr2ogr -f GeoJSON delivery_zones.geojson delivery_zones.shp # 3️⃣ Merge OSM + your polygons with tippecanoe (first convert OSM to GeoJSON) # tippecanoe can read OSM PBF directly, but you may want to filter first: osmconvert germany.osm.pbf -o=germany.osm # 4️⃣ Generate tiles (example with tippecanoe) tippecanoe \ --output=combined.pmtiles \ --layer=osm_roads --layer=osm_water --layer=osm_labels \ --layer=delivery_zones \ --drop-densest-as-needed \ --maximum-zoom=14 \ --minimum-zoom=5 \ germany.osm \ delivery_zones.geojson # 5️⃣ Serve the PMTiles file (Node example) npx pmtiles-server ./combined.pmtiles ``` > **Important:** The above commands are *illustrative*; you’ll need to tune layer filters, zoom levels, and simplification thresholds for your specific region and performance goals. The tippecanoe docs (`man tippecanoe`) and Planetiler README have extensive examples. --- ## 4️⃣ Recommended default workflow for most apps 1. **Pick a hosted vector basemap** (e.g., OpenFreeMap, MapTiler, or any public OSM vector tile service). 2. **Add your delivery-zone data**: * If it’s < 5 000 features → a simple `geojson` source (no tile server). * If it’s larger → generate a small vector-tile source just for those polygons (tippecanoe → PMTiles). 3. **Create a style** that references both sources. Insert your polygon layer *before* the first symbol layer if you want it to appear under labels. 4. **Deploy** – the map will request the basemap tiles and your overlay tiles (or GeoJSON) in parallel, and the user gets the best of both worlds: fast basemap rendering, full interactivity on your polygons, and easy updates. --- ### TL;DR Checklist - **Do you really need a single tileset?** → Only for offline/kiosk or tiny-region demos. - **Otherwise:** Use **two sources** – a basemap vector source + your own overlay (GeoJSON or vector). - **If you must merge:** 1. Get OSM extract → filter if needed. 2. Convert your polygons to GeoJSON/FlatGeobuf. 3. Merge (or just feed both to the tiler). 4. Tile with **tippecanoe** (small/medium) or **Planetiler** (large/planet). 5. Package as **PMTiles/MBTiles** (optional). 6. Host and reference in a MapLibre style. - **Remember licensing & attribution** for any OSM data you redistribute. - **Keep layers separate inside the tileset** (`source-layer` names) so you can style them independently. If you need concrete JSON for the style or help wiring the sources, check the companion skill **[maplibre-source-wiring]**. It shows exactly how to add a `vector` source (or a `geojson` source) and reference the correct `source-layer`s in your layers.

Description: explicit — vector tiles for a restylable basemap, not raw performance
prompt: I want to offer both a light and dark theme for my basemap, switchable at runtime, without hosting two separate sets of tiles. What tile type should my basemap use?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
**Use **`vector` **tiles for the basemap.**  

### Why vector tiles give you light / dark switching “for free”

| Feature | Raster tiles | Vector tiles |
|---------|--------------|--------------|
| **Separate style per theme** | You would need two complete raster tile sets (light + dark) because the colors are baked into the image. | The geometry and attributes are stored once; the map’s appearance is defined entirely by the **style JSON**. Switch the style at runtime and the same vector tiles are rendered with a light or dark palette. |
| **Bandwidth** | Two full tile pyramids → double the storage and download cost. | One tile pyramid → one request per tile regardless of theme. |
| **Client-side control** | No – the client can’t recolor raster images. | Yes – you can change any paint/layout property (background, fill, line, text, icons) on the fly, or swap the whole style object. |
| **Feature interaction** | Not queryable (no click/hover data). | Fully queryable – you still get feature properties for pop-ups, filters, etc., even when the theme changes. |
| **Future flexibility** | Adding a third theme means a third raster set. | Add any number of themes by just creating additional style JSONs (or toggling a `light/dark` flag in a single style). |

### How to implement it

1. **Serve a single vector-tile source** (e.g. a `TileJSON` URL from MapTiler, OpenFreeMap, your own PMTiles endpoint, etc.).  
   ```json
   // example source entry in a style
   "sources": {
     "basemap": {
       "type": "vector",
       "url": "https://example.com/tileset.json"
     }
   }
   ```

2. **Create two style documents** – one for the light theme, one for the dark theme.  
   *Both styles reference the same `"basemap"` source*; only the layer paint/layout values differ (background color, road colors, label colors, etc.).  

3. **Load the map with one style**, then switch at runtime:  

   ```javascript
   // initial load (light)
   const map = new maplibregl.Map({
     container: 'map',
     style: '/styles/light.json',
     center: [0, 0],
     zoom: 2
   });

   // toggle button
   document.getElementById('themeBtn').addEventListener('click', () => {
     const newStyle = map.getStyle().metadata?.theme === 'dark'
       ? '/styles/light.json'
       : '/styles/dark.json';
     map.setStyle(newStyle);
   });
   ```

   *Tip:* Store a small `metadata.theme` flag in each style so you can read the current theme without extra state.

4. **Add your own overlay sources** (GeoJSON, vector tiles, etc.) as separate sources. They will automatically inherit the new style when you call `setStyle`, or you can preserve them across style changes by using `map.once('styledata', …)` to re-add custom layers.

### Edge cases & best-practice notes

| Situation | Recommendation |
|-----------|----------------|
| **You need satellite imagery** | Keep the satellite imagery as a **raster** source (e.g., `raster` tiles) and overlay the vector basemap (light/dark) on top. The raster source is independent of the theme. |
| **Offline kiosk with no network** | Bundle a single vector tile archive (e.g., a PMTiles file) and ship two lightweight style JSONs. No extra tile storage is required. |
| **Very low-end devices** | Vector tiles are still smaller than raster equivalents, but you may want to limit the max zoom or simplify the source-layer data to keep parsing fast. |
| **You only have a raster basemap** | You would have to generate a second raster set for the opposite theme; this defeats the “single-source” goal. Consider switching to a vector basemap provider (MapTiler, OpenStreetMap-based tiles, etc.) instead. |

### TL;DR

- **Tile type:** `vector`
- **Why:** One vector tile set can be styled any number of ways; you just swap the style JSON (light ↔ dark) at runtime.
- **What you need:** a single vector-tile source + two style documents (light & dark). No extra tile storage, no extra network requests beyond the style switch.
